issues.issue: The closing sentence directs that "[a]ny inconsistencies or ambiguities in this Agreement" be resolved to preserve the REMIC elections, a self-referential interpretive command whose reach over the operative distribution provisions is itself uncertain. A court could be asked to decide how far that instruction overrides otherwise plain terms.

Clause (iv) reads "until the principal balance of such Subsidiary REMIC Regular Interest the Subordinated Portion for Loan Group 3," omitting the verb "equals" that appears in every parallel clause. The omission leaves the fourth priority without a stated stopping point on its face.

The Class P Prepayment Charges are here distributed to the LT-Group interests, while Section 4.02(b) directs the same charges to the Class P Certificates and Section 3.07(k) holds them in the Class P Reserve Fund. Reconciling the REMIC-level deemed distributions with the certificate-level distributions requires construction.

Clause (iv) omits the verb "equals" ("until the principal balance of such Middle REMIC 1 Regular Interest the Subordinated Portion for Loan Group 3"). The fourth priority therefore lacks a stated cap on its face.

The table contains transcription defects that change stated amounts and rates, notably the Class X-2 Notional Amount given as "$452,182,00" and the Class 2-A-1 rate footnote reference "Variable(2". A dollar figure missing a digit is a mechanical error going to the size of an entitlement.

After four enumerated categories the definition adds "and, in general, any Certificates that do not satisfy the applicable ratings requirement under the Underwriter's Exemption," a catch-all qualified by the wholly indeterminate phrase "in general." Whether a given Class falls inside that residual category cannot be answered from the text.

"Physical Certificates" is limited to the Class C, Class P and Residual Certificates, yet Section 5.02(e) and the definition of Definitive Certificates contemplate physical certificates being issued for Book-Entry Classes. The two provisions cannot both be read literally.

"Defined terms and provisions herein relating to statistical rating agencies not designated above" is a blanket nullification whose target provisions are nowhere identified. Which references it strikes out is left to inference.

"Control" is the pivot of clause (i) ("directly or indirectly controls or is controlled by or is under common control with") but is nowhere defined, and clause (ii) extends the term to anyone serving "in a similar capacity." Both phrases have contestable boundaries.

The definition duplicates the phrase "with respect to such Mortgage Loan at the close of business on the related Servicer Remittance Date," leaving the measuring date stated twice and the sentence ungrammatical. The repetition obscures what is actually being aggregated.

For a Refinancing Mortgage Loan the value is the origination appraisal "as modified by an updated appraisal," without saying when, by whom or on what basis such an update is made. The qualifier has no ascertainable boundary.

The cross-reference "Section 3.22(i)(a)" inverts the subsection labels; the Assessment of Compliance is in fact defined in Section 3.22(a)(i). The citation as written points to a subsection that does not exist.

The Certificate Insurer becomes Auction Initiator only if the Class C holder "has not exercised its rights ... on any date on which [it] is entitled to do so," a condition that never closes because further such dates keep arising. When the substitution takes effect cannot be fixed from the words.

Available Funds is defined only "as to any Distribution Date and any Loan Group," but Section 4.02(a) and the Preliminary Statement direct the Trust Administrator to withdraw and apply "the Available Funds" on an aggregate basis. The single-group definition does not fit the aggregate usage.

The definition uses the labels (a) and (b) twice in the same sentence, once for the outer "lesser of" and again inside clause (b), so "(a) the Principal Funds" and "(b) the Overcollateralization Release Amount" collide with the outer clauses. The reader must guess which pair is meant.

This general definition of Business Day (New York, Minnesota, Maryland and the Corporate Trust Office cities) is contradicted by Section 12.04(j), which defines "Business Day" for Article XII by reference only to New York and the Corporate Trust Office of the Master Servicer, Trustee or Trust Administrator. The two definitions can produce different days.

The Agreement defines only "Cap Contract Termination Date," but Sections 3.24, 3.10(d) and 4.07(a) all operate by reference to a "Cap Contract Scheduled Termination Date" that is never defined. Whether the two are the same term is left to inference.

The Cap Provider is defined as Swiss Re Financial Products Corporation, yet Section 3.24 imposes the post-termination payment obligation on a "Cap Contract Counterparty" that the Agreement never defines. The identity of the obligor rests on equating two different labels.

The definition points to "Section 12.04(j)" for Certificate Insurer Default, but the term is actually created in the first sentence of Section 12.01; Section 12.04(j) deals with "Receipt" and Business Days. The cross-reference leads nowhere.

The two margin columns turn entirely on the "Optional Termination Date," which the definitions section defines only "[a]s specified in Section 10.01(a)," and Section 10.01(a) never specifies any such date. The step-up trigger therefore has no ascertainable date behind it.

"Certification: As specified in Section 9.12(d)" misdirects: the Sarbanes-Oxley Certification is created in Section 9.12(b)(iv), while Section 9.12(d) concerns late filings and amendments. The defined term has no source where it points.

The tail of the definition sweeps in "any amounts with respect to the Class 1-A-3 Certificates owing to the Certificate Insurer and remaining unpaid," a residual category with no stated source of the obligation. What amounts qualify cannot be determined from the words.

As with the parallel Class 1-A-3 definition, the closing words capture "any amounts ... owing to the Certificate Insurer and remaining unpaid" without identifying the obligations meant. The catch-all's reach is indeterminate.

The definition ends with an open-ended catch-all for "any amounts with respect to the Class 4-A-2 Certificates owing to the Certificate Insurer and remaining unpaid," leaving the covered obligations unspecified. Its scope is a matter of construction.

Compensating Interest is defined solely by reference to the Servicers' obligations, yet Section 3.02(f) imposes the payment on the Master Servicer if a Servicer fails and Section 4.04(a)(xvii) cites "Section 3.24" (the Cap Contract) as the source of such payments. The definition and its operative cross-references do not line up.

The definition describes a Cooperative Mortgage Loan as secured by "a second lien on and a perfected security interest in Cooperative Shares," although the delivery and representation provisions treat these loans as first-priority collateral. "Second lien" appears to be a drafting slip that changes the described security.

The defined term is "Countrywide Mortgage Loans," but the Countrywide Servicing Agreement definition and Section 2.01 refer to "Countrywide Serviced Mortgage Loans." The Agreement uses two labels for what appears to be one pool.

"Covered" is defined only by pointing to Appendix E of an external and undated "Standard & Poor's Glossary," so the content of the category is fixed outside the instrument. Which loans qualify cannot be read off the Agreement.

The fee is computed on the "Scheduled Principal Balance of the Mortgage Loans," a term the Agreement never defines; the defined balance concepts are "Principal Balance" and "Stated Principal Balance." The multiplicand of the fee is therefore not fixed by the instrument.

Current Interest is defined only "[w]ith respect to each Class of Offered Certificates," yet Section 4.02(a)(4) and Section 4.04(a)(xvi) compute Current Interest for the Class M-8 and Class C Certificates, which are not Offered Certificates. The definition does not cover classes the distribution waterfall applies it to.

Definitive Certificates are defined as "[a]ny Physical Certificate issued pursuant to Section 5.02(e)," but Physical Certificates are defined as only the Class C, Class P and Residual Certificates, whereas Section 5.02(e) issues Definitive Certificates on collapse of the book-entry system for Book-Entry Classes. The two definitions cannot both stand.

The trigger turns on the "Rolling Sixty Day Delinquency Rate," a capitalised term that appears nowhere else in the Agreement and is never defined in Section 1.01. The measure that switches the waterfall from the stepdown priorities is thus supplied from outside the instrument.

The Determination Date is defined only as "[t]he date on which a Servicer is required to determine" its advance under "the applicable Servicing Agreement," which yields a different date for each of the five Servicers. Provisions such as Section 2.03 and Section 10.01 nevertheless speak of a single "Determination Date."

Condition (vi) requires the substitute loan to be "the same credit grade category as the Deleted Mortgage Loan," but the Agreement nowhere establishes credit grade categories. Whether a proffered loan satisfies the condition cannot be determined from the text.

Condition (v) requires compliance with "each representation and warranty set forth in Section 2.03 hereof," yet Section 2.03 sets forth no loan-level representations; they are made in Schedule II and merely incorporated by that Section. The pointer misses its target.

The definition lists the Final Certification's recipients as the Depositor, Trustee and Transferor, while Section 2.02 requires delivery also to the Certificate Insurer. The two statements of the same obligation do not match.

The formula subtracts a dollar amount ("the sum of Current Interest for the Class X-1 Certificates and the Group 1 XW Amount") from a per annum rate (the Net WAC) before the numbered steps "multiplied by 12" and "divided by the Stated Principal Balance," so the stated order of operations cannot be performed as written. The cap can be computed only by rearranging the words.

After naming specific statutory categories, clause (b) extends to any "'predatory' or similar loan under any other applicable state, federal or local law," together with a parenthetical reaching "similarly classified" loans "using different terminology." The residual language leaves the class of covered loans open-ended.

"Highest Priority" is fixed by reference to "the highest priority for payments pursuant to Section 4.01," but Section 4.01 governs Advances and contains no payment priorities; the priorities are in Section 4.02. The definition points at the wrong operative provision.

The category is defined wholly by an external, undated source, "Appendix E of Standard & Poor's Glossary," so the content of "Home Loan" is not ascertainable from the Agreement. Its boundaries depend on a document outside the deal.

Clause (a) requires only that the Person be "in fact independent," a standard with no stated content, and clause (d) refers to "a Person defined clause (b) or (c) above," which is both ungrammatical and mismatched because (b) and (c) define no Person. The test is not applicable as written.

The definition is circular and unbounded: an Insurance Policy is "any insurance policy" relating to a Mortgage Loan "including any replacement policy or policies for any Insurance Policies." Nothing in the words limits which policies are captured.

"Expenses covered by an Insurance Policy or any other insurance policy with respect to the Mortgage Loans" defines the term by a catch-all that swallows the specific reference preceding it. Which expenses are reimbursable under Section 3.10(a)(iv) is left open.

The term is defined "[a]s defined in Section 2.01(c)," but Section 2.01(c) creates and names the "Trust" and never uses the phrase "Issuing Entity," which Section 9.12 then employs for the Exchange Act filings. The definition has no referent.

The rate is capped by reference to "the Insured Notes" and to a maximum "as determined by the Class A Note Insurer," neither of which is a defined term or an identified party anywhere in this Agreement. The ceiling on the Late Payment Rate owed to the Certificate Insurer therefore cannot be computed from the instrument.

The formula (three years after the latest scheduled maturity as of the Cut-off Date) must be squared with the Preliminary Statement and Section 10.01(a), which fix the Latest Possible Maturity Date as December 25, 2046 for every Class. Whether the formula or the stated date governs is left open.

"Majority Holder" is defined in words identical to "Majority in Interest," creating two labels for one concept and no guide to which governs where the Agreement uses one rather than the other. The duplication invites argument over whether a difference was intended.

The definition is expressed only "[a]s to any Class of Regular Certificates," yet Section 11.02 requires the direction of a "Majority in Interest of the Certificateholders" across all Classes. The definition does not fit that use.

The defined term is "Master Servicer Compensation," but Section 3.19 entitles the Master Servicer to withdraw "the Master Servicing Compensation," a differently named term that Section 1.01 does not define. The compensation actually payable rests on equating the two labels.

Only a "Mezzanine Cap Contract Termination Date" is defined, whereas Sections 3.25, 3.10(e) and 4.08(a) operate by reference to a "Mezzanine Cap Contract Scheduled Termination Date" that appears nowhere in Section 1.01. The date on which those provisions cut off is supplied only by inference.

The provider is identified as Swiss Re Financial Products Corporation, but Section 3.25 imposes the termination payment on an undefined "Mezzanine Cap Contract Counterparty." The obligor is named by one term in the definitions and another in the operative section.

Within clause (b) the drafter re-uses the labels "(a)" and "(b)" that already designate the outer "excess of" limbs, so the "lesser of (a) the product ... and (b) the aggregate Stated Principal Balance" collides with the outer structure. The formula must be reconstructed to be applied.

The Mortgage is defined as the instrument "creating a second lien" on the mortgaged estate, which describes junior-lien collateral in a transaction whose conveyance and insurance provisions treat the loans as the trust's primary security. The lien position stated is at odds with the instrument the definition is meant to describe.

Items (5) and (7) of the schedule are keyed to the "Scheduled Principal Balance" of each Mortgage Loan, a term the Agreement never defines even though it also defines "Principal Balance" and "Stated Principal Balance." The required content of the Schedule therefore rests on an undefined measure.

Mortgaged Property is limited to one- to four-family dwellings and condominium units, yet the Agreement expressly contemplates Cooperative Mortgage Loans whose collateral is shares and a Proprietary Lease rather than such property. The definition does not cover a category of loans the deal includes.

The NIMS Insurer is defined as "[a]ny insurer" guaranteeing notes secured by certain Certificates, without identifying anyone or providing for how the parties are to know whether such an insurer exists at a given time. Dozens of consent and notice rights turn on that indeterminate identification.

Whether an Advance is nonrecoverable rests entirely on the Servicer's or Master Servicer's own "good faith judgment" that it "will not be ultimately recoverable ... from the related Mortgagor, related Liquidation Proceeds or otherwise," with "or otherwise" left open. Both the standard and the sources of recovery are contestable.

The notice is said to be given "pursuant to Section 10.02," but the notice of final distribution requiring surrender of Certificates is provided for in Section 10.01(d); Section 10.02 contains only the REMIC qualified-liquidation requirements. The cross-reference does not match the operative text.

The Class C Notional Amount is measured by "the aggregate Uncertificated Balance of the Middle REMIC 2 Regular Interests," but "Uncertificated Balance" is never defined in Section 1.01 or the Preliminary Statement, which speak instead of principal balances. The measure of the Class C notional rests on an undefined term.

The Officer's Certificate may be signed only by officers "of the Depositor or the Master Servicer," although Sections 6.05 and 8.02 contemplate Officer's Certificates from other parties. The definition does not reach every use the Agreement makes of the term.

The definition is entirely derivative — "[a]s specified in Section 10.01(a)" — but Section 10.01(a) never specifies an Optional Termination Date. The Certificate Margin step-up and other provisions keyed to that date have no fixed referent.

An Order is defined by reference to the return of a "Preference Amount," a capitalised term that is used nowhere else and never defined; Article XII speaks instead of a "Preference Claim." The trigger for the definition rests on a term the Agreement does not supply.

The definition breaks off mid-clause — "over (ii) the Overcollateralization Target Amount for such Distribution" — leaving the second limb of the excess incomplete. As written the amount cannot be computed.

After ten enumerated categories the list closes with "(k) such other investments ... acceptable to each Rating Agency," an open residual category that is not limited by the kinds of instruments enumerated. Whether an investment outside (a)-(j) qualifies turns on that catch-all.

Limb (B) adds "the Premium Distribution Amount for any prior Distribution Date, plus interest thereon," without limiting it to any portion that remains unpaid, so on its face every prior period's premium is re-added each month. The compounding that results is plainly not what the formula is meant to do.

The definition twice turns on a "Liquidated Loan," a term Section 1.01 does not define; the defined concept is "Liquidated Mortgage Loan." Whether the two are identical determines when a loan's Principal Balance drops to zero.

The Principal Remittance Amount is defined for the pool as a whole, yet the Group Principal Distribution Amount definitions and Section 4.02 all operate on a "Principal Remittance Amount for Loan Group 1" (and 2, 3 and 4). The allocation among Loan Groups is not supplied by the definition.

The Purchase Price includes "any costs and damages incurred by the Trust in connection with any violation by such Mortgage Loan of any predatory or abusive lending law," a component with no stated measure, cap or time limit. What a repurchasing Transferor must pay is left open.

The Agreement separately defines "Qualified Insurer" with detailed licensing and rating requirements and "Qualified Mortgage Insurer" as merely any GSE-approved insurer, and uses the latter in the Mortgage Loan Schedule. Which standard governs a given insurance policy is not resolved.

The second sentence applies to No Delay Certificates "held in Book-Entry Form," an undefined phrase, and the first sentence covers Delay Certificates "or Physical Certificates," categories that overlap, leaving no rule for a No Delay Certificate held in definitive form. The Record Date for that case is unstated.
The definition stops in mid-sentence at "issued after," so the cut-off date that gives the term its entire content is missing. A REMIC Change of Law cannot be identified from the words.

The definition lists many officer titles and then adds "any other officer ... customarily performing functions similar to those performed by any of the above designated officers having direct responsibility for the administration of this Agreement and also to whom ... such matter is referred because of such officer's knowledge," so it is unclear whether the responsibility and referral qualifiers attach to every listed officer or only to the residual category. Trustee liability for "actual knowledge of a Responsible Officer" turns on that reading.

The term is defined with hyphens as "Rolling Sixty-Day Delinquency Rate," while the Delinquency Trigger Event definition operates on a "Rolling Sixty Day Delinquency Rate." The trigger depends on treating the two spellings as the same defined term.

If a change in law makes certification "materially more onerous," the required certification becomes whatever is "agreed to by the Master Servicer and the Depositor following a negotiation in good faith" — an agreement to agree, with the onerousness judged by the Master Servicer itself. The content of the obligation is left undetermined.

The Scheduled Payment is to give effect to "any related Debt Service Reduction," but Debt Service Reduction is never defined in Section 1.01 and appears nowhere else in the Agreement. The adjustment to every monthly payment rests on an undefined term.

The Servicers are listed as six entities including Cenlar, but the Assignment Agreements definition covers only five (AHM, Countrywide, IndyMac, GMACM and RFC), so the Cenlar loans are not within the assignment structure Section 2.01 relies on. The two definitions describe different servicing populations.

Servicing Advances are limited to "customary, reasonable and necessary" out-of-pocket costs incurred in performing servicing obligations, three overlapping and undefined qualifiers. Whether a particular expense is reimbursable turns on standards the Agreement does not fix.

The closing sentence sets the balance of a "Liquidated Loan" at zero, but the Agreement defines only "Liquidated Mortgage Loan." The point at which a loan drops out of every balance-based calculation depends on an undefined label.

The definition applies to a Mortgage Loan "purchased by the originator," although the shortfall it measures arises on substitution by the Transferor, and the sentence lacks a verb linking the subject to "is an amount equal to." As written the trigger and the actor are both wrong.

Section 2.03 defines the Substitution Adjustment Amount as the aggregate shortfall determined by the Master Servicer and requires the Transferor also to remit unreimbursed Advances, which this loan-by-loan definition omits. The two statements of the same amount differ.

The Supplemental Interest Trust Trustee is said to act "for the benefit of the Holders of the Certificates," whereas Section 4.06 and the Supplemental Interest Trust definition confine the beneficiaries to holders of the Senior and Mezzanine Certificates. The class of beneficiaries differs between the two provisions.

The Termination Price is said to be defined in Section 10.01(d), but that subsection deals with notice of liquidation; the price is defined in Section 10.01(c). The cross-reference points to the wrong subsection.

Clause (c) includes the Policy Payments Account "and all amounts deposited therein" in the Trust Fund, while Section 12.06 states that neither the Certificate Insurance Policy nor amounts paid on it constitute part of the Trust Fund. The two provisions cannot both be right about the same money.

Voting Rights are allocated among the Senior, Mezzanine and Class C holders "in proportion to the then outstanding Certificate Principal Balances," but the Interest Only Certificates are Senior Certificates that by definition have no Certificate Principal Balance. On the face of the definition they are given a share of the 98% and receive none.

The grant and the proviso use the same labels (i) and (ii) for different conditions, and the parenthetical exception is expressed "in the case of clause (ii) below" when clause (ii) has already been used above, so it cannot be told which condition the exception attaches to. Whether the NIMS Insurer holds rights at a given moment is not determinable from the text.

The whole provision turns on notes "issued pursuant to the Indenture," but "Indenture" is nowhere defined in this Agreement even though Sections 10.01(b) and (c) also condition termination on it. The condition precedent to the NIMS Insurer's rights is supplied by an instrument the Agreement never identifies.

The long parenthetical carving out retained Servicer rights leaves the sentence with unclosed parentheses and no clear object, so exactly which "right, title and interest" passes to the Trustee — and which was "retained by the Transferor pursuant to the Assignment Agreements" — is unclear on the face of the granting clause. The scope of the conveyance is the point most likely to be argued.

Clause (A) requires an endorsement "in blank" but prescribes the form "Pay to the order of ___________ without recourse," and clauses (B), (C) and (E) are all qualified by "except as provided below." What the Custodian must actually hold for a given loan is not fixed by this clause alone.

Clause (F) refers to "the security interest referenced in clause (v) above," but this list is lettered (A) through (H) and contains no clause (v). The document the Custodian must hold cannot be identified from the cross-reference.

The paragraph states that "in no event" shall delivery of the original Mortgage and interim assignments be later than one year after the Closing Date, and then immediately allows delivery "within 720 days following the Closing Date" if the recording office has not returned the documents. The absolute outer limit contradicts the proviso in the same sentence.

The recording carve-outs turn on whether recordation is required "by either Rating Agency," although the Preliminary Statement designates three Rating Agencies (Moody's, S&P and Fitch), and the closing sentence breaks off mid-clause ("may conclusively 47"). Both the number of rating agencies and the scope of the reliance are left uncertain.

The parties merely "agree and understand that it is not intended that any Loan be included" in the five listed high-cost categories, which states an intention rather than a covenant or warranty, yet an indemnity is attached to "the provisions of the preceding sentence." Whether the sentence creates an enforceable obligation at all is open.

This subsection is reproduced word for word as Section 3.07(g), so the same Eligible Account requirement appears twice in the instrument. Duplicated operative text raises the question whether the two are meant to have different effect.

The repurchase obligation is triggered by failure to cure within ninety days of "the earlier of its discovery or its receipt of written notice" of a defect that "materially and adversely affects the interests of the Certificateholders," without defining discovery or the materiality measure. Both phrases determine whether and when a repurchase duty ever arises.

This paragraph gives only repurchase at the Purchase Price for uncured document defects, while the sole-remedy sentence at the end of Section 2.02 assumes the Transferor may instead "substitute ... an Eligible Substitute Mortgage Loan." The remedy stated and the remedy preserved do not match.

The clause makes repurchase or substitution the "sole remedies" for a document defect and lists only the Trustee, the Master Servicer, the Depositor and any Certificateholder as bound by that limitation. Whether the limitation also binds the Certificate Insurer and the NIMS Insurer, who are omitted, is a question the enumeration itself raises.

Section 11.12 makes the Certificate Insurer and the NIMS Insurer third-party beneficiaries "to the same extent as if [they] were a party hereto," with the right to enforce the Agreement, which sits awkwardly with a sole-remedy clause that does not mention them. The two provisions pull in different directions on those parties' remedies.

For knowledge-qualified representations the provision deems an inaccuracy a breach "notwithstanding the Transferor's lack of knowledge," which reads the knowledge qualifier out of the very representations to which it applies. The interaction between the qualifier and the deeming sentence is genuinely contestable.

The Trustee must enforce the cure obligation and act "if the Transferor fails to correct or cure the defect within such period," but no period is stated anywhere in this paragraph, so "such period" has no antecedent. The time the Transferor has to cure cannot be found in the provision that turns on it.

The ninety-day cure clock runs from "the earlier of its discovery or its receipt of written notice" of a breach that "materially and adversely affects the interest of the Certificateholders," and neither "discovery" nor the materiality standard is defined. When the repurchase obligation matures turns on those words.

This paragraph defines the Substitution Adjustment Amount as an aggregate shortfall determined by the Master Servicer and adds unreimbursed Advances, whereas the Section 1.01 definition of the same term measures a single loan's shortfall on purchase "by the originator." The two definitions of one term differ.

The sole-remedy sentence lists the Certificateholders, Master Servicer, NIMS Insurer, Depositor, Trust Administrator and Trustee, but omits the Certificate Insurer, to whom the representations in Section 2.03 are expressly made. The omission from an otherwise exhaustive list invites an expressio unius argument about whose remedies are cut off.

A breach of the Depositor's Section 2.04 title representation requires only notice; unlike Sections 2.02 and 2.03 the Agreement provides no cure, repurchase or substitution remedy against the Depositor. The instrument creates a warranty with no stated consequence.

The Trustee agrees "to perform the duties set forth in this Agreement to the best of its ability, to the end that the interests of the Holders ... may be adequately and effectively protected," which cannot easily be squared with Section 8.01, under which the Trustee performs "only such duties as are specifically set forth" and "no implied covenants or obligations shall be read into this Agreement against the Trustee." The scope of the Trustee's pre-default duty is left in genuine doubt.

The Master Servicer must act "with customary and usual standards of practice of prudent mortgage loan master servicers" while also having "full power and authority to do any and all things which it may deem necessary or desirable," two standards of very different content applied to the same conduct. What the Master Servicer was actually required to do is left to be construed.

The paragraph provides that servicing costs shall not be added to "the Scheduled Principal Balances of the related Mortgage Loans," a term the Agreement never defines; the defined balances are "Principal Balance" and "Stated Principal Balance." The measure the limitation operates on is missing.

Whether a Servicer is to be terminated is left to the Master Servicer's own "judgment," and it may then "take such other action as it deems appropriate," with no standard against which either determination can be tested. The obligation is measured entirely by the obligor's own view.

Enforcement must be carried out "to such an extent and at such time as the Master Servicer, in its good faith business judgment, would require were it the owner of the related Mortgage Loans," a hypothetical-owner standard whose content is indeterminate. It sits alongside an apparently mandatory duty to terminate a defaulting Servicer.

This subsection makes the Master Servicer the backstop payer of Compensating Interest, but Section 4.04(a)(xvii) describes such payments as made "by the Servicer pursuant to Section 3.24," which is the Cap Contract provision. The Agreement points to two different sources for the same obligation.

The Master Servicer must evaluate a Servicer's consent request "in the best interest of the Trust and the Certificateholders" and "grant or withhold such consent accordingly," without any criterion for identifying that interest among differently situated Classes. The standard governing the decision is open-ended.

The flat statement that neither the Trustee nor the Depositor has "any responsibility or liability for any action or failure to act by the Master Servicer" must be read against Section 7.02 and Section 3.05, under which the Trustee succeeds to and is liable for the master servicing function after an Event of Termination. The disclaimer is broader than the rest of the instrument allows.

Exception (i) relieves the Trustee of liability "for losses of the predecessor Master Servicer pursuant to Section 3.09 hereof," but Section 3.09 concerns access to documentation and imposes no loss liability. The carve-out points to a provision that cannot support it.

Clauses (x) and (xi) require deposit of amounts "in respect of the Mortgage Loans in such Loan Group," but no Loan Group has been identified anywhere in the subsection, and clause (xii) closes with the open catch-all "any other amounts required to be deposited hereunder." Neither the antecedent nor the residual category can be fixed from the text.

The closing sentence provides that "[i]n the absence of written instructions by the Trust Administrator, all funds on deposit therein shall remain uninvested," although the Collection Account is invested at the written direction of the Master Servicer, so "therein" cannot refer to both accounts consistently. Which account is left uninvested, and on whose default, is unclear.

Investment income on the Collection Account is said to belong to the Master Servicer "as Master Servicing Compensation," whereas Section 1.01 defines only "Master Servicer Compensation." The entitlement is expressed in a term the definitions do not contain.

This subsection repeats Section 2.01(e) essentially verbatim, so the Agreement contains the same Eligible Account covenant twice. Duplicated operative text raises a question whether some difference was intended.

The Carryover Reserve Fund is established "in trust for the benefit of the Holders of the Offered Certificates," yet investments in it are made "for the benefit of the Holders of the Class C Certificates," who are also said to own the fund for tax purposes and to direct its investment. The identity of the beneficiaries is stated two different ways in one subsection.

The exculpation applies to investments "made in accordance with this Section 3.05," but this is Section 3.07(h); Section 3.05 concerns the Trustee acting as Master Servicer. The protection is tied to the wrong provision.

The Mezzanine Cap Account is held for the benefit of the Holders of the Mezzanine Certificates, but Sections 3.10(e) and 4.08 direct its funds to the Mezzanine Certificates and the Class C Certificates. The stated beneficiaries and the stated distributees differ.

Sub-clause (iii) permits reimbursement of "any Nonrecoverable Advance previously made" from the Collection Account generally, with no limitation to collections on the related Mortgage Loan, in contrast to the express limits written into sub-clauses (ii) and (v). Whether that reimbursement may be taken from unrelated collections is left to construction.

Clause (iii) allows the whole balance of the Carryover Reserve Fund to be distributed to the Depositor "after the distribution of any Net Rate Carryover to the Certificates on the Distribution Date in December of 2006," which on its face empties the fund on the second Distribution Date of the deal. The date appears to be a mechanical error that destroys the fund's stated purpose.

Read literally, this clause releases the $2,380,000 Carryover Reserve Fund to the Depositor in December 2006, which cannot be reconciled with Section 3.07(h) and Section 4.02(a), under which the fund exists to pay Net Rate Carryover to the Offered Certificates over the life of the deal. The provisions cannot both operate.

The Cap Account is to be cleared on "the Cap Contract Scheduled Termination Date," a term never defined; Section 1.01 defines only "Cap Contract Termination Date." The date on which the account terminates rests on equating the two.

The clause operates on the "Mezzanine Cap Contract Scheduled Termination Date," which the Agreement never defines; Section 1.01 defines only "Mezzanine Cap Contract Termination Date." The termination date of the account is not supplied by the instrument.

The Master Servicer must use its "best reasonable efforts" to keep primary mortgage insurance in force, a hybrid of two different and undefined effort standards. What level of effort was owed is exactly the kind of question that has to be construed.

Foreclosure is required for loans "as to which no satisfactory arrangements can be made for collection of delinquent payments," without saying satisfactory to whom or by what measure. The trigger for the duty is unascertainable on its face.

REO Property must be sold "as expeditiously as possible" but only "to the extent provided in the applicable Servicing Agreement" and "in accordance with" that agreement, so an absolute-sounding standard is qualified by five separate servicing contracts. The obligation's content cannot be fixed from this provision.

The Master Servicer's entire compensation is defined as "the Master Servicing Compensation," but Section 1.01 defines only "Master Servicer Compensation" (investment earnings on the Collection Account). The sole compensation provision rests on a term the definitions section does not contain.

Clause (C) fixes the assessment period by reference to "the Form 10 K required to be filed pursuant to Section 3.22," but no Form 10-K is required by Section 3.22; the filing obligation is in Section 9.12(b). The period covered by the assessment is tied to a non-existent requirement.

The parties' obligations "will be supplemented and modified as necessary to be consistent with" amendments, "interpretive advice or guidance, convention or consensus among active participants in the asset-backed securities markets, advice of counsel, or otherwise," and compliance is owed only "to the extent practicable from a timing and information systems perspective." Both the trigger and the measure of the duty are indeterminate.

The required errors and omissions policy and fidelity bond must be "in such form and such amount generally acceptable for entities serving as master servicer," with no amount, no rating requirement and no party to determine acceptability. The coverage actually owed cannot be derived from the words.

This Section assigns the Cap Contract deposit function to the Supplemental Interest Trust Trustee, while Section 2.01(f) directs the Trust Administrator to "execute, deliver and perform its obligations under the Cap Contract" and Section 3.07(i) requires the Trust Administrator to deposit Cap Contract receipts. The same function is given to two capacities.

The paragraph turns on "the Confirmation," the "Cap Contract Counterparty" and the "Cap Contract Scheduled Termination Date," none of which is defined in Section 1.01 (which defines only the Cap Provider and the Cap Contract Termination Date). The events of termination, the obligor and the end date all rest on undefined labels.

The final sentence asks whether termination amounts "remain in the Cap Account," although the entire paragraph concerns the Mezzanine Cap Contract and the Mezzanine Cap Account. The wrong account is named in the provision that disposes of the money.

The Credit Risk Manager "may be terminated by the Depositor at the direction of Certificateholders evidencing not less than 66 2/3% of the Voting Rights" only "[i]f the Credit Risk Manager is no longer able to perform its duties hereunder," a condition with no stated measure that appears to be the sole ground of removal. Whether holders can remove for poor performance turns on that phrase.

The Master Servicer's advancing duty is excused "to the extent the Master Servicer determines any such Advance to be a Nonrecoverable Advance," leaving the obligation measured by the obligor's own determination, supported only by an Officer's Certificate "detailing the reason(s)." Whether an advance was properly withheld turns on that self-judging standard.

Class P Prepayment Charges are here withdrawn from the Distribution Account and paid to the Class P Certificates, while the Preliminary Statement deems the same charges distributed through the REMIC interests to the MT2-Q Interest and Section 3.07(k) establishes a separate Class P Reserve Fund for those Certificates. The routes the charges take are described inconsistently.

The opening words require the principal and interest figures in clauses (i) and (ii) to be "expressed as a dollar amount per one thousand," while the closing sentence of the same subsection requires the identical information to be "expressed as a dollar amount per single Certificate of the relevant Class." The subsection gives two incompatible measures for the same disclosure.

Clause (xvii) excludes Prepayment Interest Shortfalls "covered by payments by the Servicer pursuant to Section 3.24," but Section 3.24 is the Cap Contract provision; Compensating Interest is dealt with in Section 3.02(f) and the Servicing Agreements. The exclusion points to an unrelated section.

The Trust Administrator's responsibility is said to be "limited to the availability, timeliness and the accuracy of the information provided by each Servicer," which read literally makes it responsible for the Servicers' accuracy rather than excusing it, the opposite of the sentence's evident purpose and of the later disclaimer in the same subsection. The limitation can be read two ways.

The Supplemental Interest Trust is held "for the benefit of the holders of the Senior Certificates and the Mezzanine Certificates," whereas the definition of Supplemental Interest Trust Trustee says it acts "for the benefit of the Holders of the Certificates." The beneficiary class is described differently in the two places.

The opening words limit Cap Account distributions to what is "needed to pay any Unpaid Realized Loss Amount or Net Rate Carryover," but the first two priorities pay an Overcollateralization Deficiency Amount and Interest Carry Forward Amounts, which are neither; the priorities are also mis-numbered, running (11) through (18) and then (9). The stated purpose and the enumerated priorities do not match.

The whole section operates "on or prior to the ... Cap Contract Scheduled Termination Date," a term the Agreement never defines, Section 1.01 defining only the "Cap Contract Termination Date." The period during which the Cap Account is distributed rests on an undefined date.

The section runs to the "Mezzanine Cap Contract Scheduled Termination Date," which is not a defined term; Section 1.01 defines only the "Mezzanine Cap Contract Termination Date." The cut-off for these distributions is not supplied by the instrument.

The MTA fallback uses "the Reserve Interest Rate," but that term is created and defined only in Section 4.10 in the context of LIBOR quotations for one-month dollar deposits, and Section 1.01 does not define it. The substitute rate for MTA Certificates depends on borrowing a definition from a different index provision.

On a failure of the index the Trust Administrator must choose "a new index ... that is based on comparable information" and adjust the margin by reference to "MTA for the final three years it was in effect," with no criteria for comparability and no procedure or consent requirement. The rate payable on the MTA Certificates would then be set by an undefined standard.

COFI is to be taken from the FHLB statistics "as most recently available generally as of a day specified in the related note," a phrase that identifies neither the day nor which "note" is meant in a provision about certificates. The measurement date cannot be fixed from the words.

The COFI fallback rate is "the Reserve Interest Rate," which is defined only in Section 4.10 by reference to one-month dollar lending rates quoted for LIBOR purposes and is not defined in Section 1.01. The substitute rate for COFI Certificates is imported from an unrelated index mechanism.

The Trust Administrator must select "a new index for the COFI Certificates that is based on comparable information" and adjust the margin using "COFI for the final three years it was in effect," with no standard of comparability and no third-party check. The interest rate on a Class of Certificates would be set by an undefined discretion.

Denominations are to be "the minimum denominations, integral multiples ... and aggregate denominations per Class set forth in the Preliminary Statement," but the Preliminary Statement sets out only designations, rates and initial balances and states no minimum denominations. The provision points to information the referenced text does not contain.

For an ERISA-Restricted Certificate that is neither a Private nor a Residual Certificate the required representation "shall be deemed to have been made" by acceptance, yet the same paragraph declares any transfer "in violation of the above restrictions" void; a deemed representation and a voidness rule cannot both govern the same transfer. Which controls a transfer to a Plan is unresolved.

The transfer restriction applies only "prior to the termination of the Interest Rate Cap Agreement," but the Agreement defines no such instrument; the hedges here are the "Cap Contract" and the "Mezzanine Cap Contract." The date on which this restriction lapses cannot be identified.

Access to the holder list requires "three or more Certificateholders" who "state that such Certificateholders desire to communicate" and supply the proposed communication, without saying whether the Trust Administrator may test those statements or refuse a request. The conditions on a holder's access right are the kind of thing parties fight over.

A merger successor becomes the Master Servicer automatically "without the execution or filing of any paper ... anything herein to the contrary notwithstanding," while Section 6.05 subjects any transfer of the master servicing to net worth, rating-agency and opinion conditions and Section 11.07 requires consents. The instrument provides two inconsistent routes to the same result.

The exculpation is expressed only as freedom from "liability to the Trust" for good-faith action, leaving open whether the same parties remain liable to Certificateholders or the Certificate Insurer for the same conduct. The class of protected claims is not stated.

Condition (i) is stated disjunctively — the transferee "(a) shall be a Person qualified to service ... for Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac, (b) shall have a net worth of not less than $50,000,000 ... or (c) shall execute and deliver ... an assumption agreement" — so on its face a transferee satisfying only (a) or only (b) need not assume the Master Servicer's obligations. The "or" appears to be a mechanical error that guts the condition.

This Section permits the Master Servicer to sell or delegate its rights and duties on satisfying rating and net worth conditions, whereas Section 11.07 provides that the Agreement "may not be assigned by the Master Servicer without the prior written consent of the Trustee, the Certificate Insurer and Depositor." The two provisions state different requirements for the same transaction.

Clause (v) makes it an Event of Termination for the Master Servicer to assign or delegate "in contravention of the provisions permitting such assignment or delegation under Section 6.04," but Section 6.04 governs resignation; assignment and delegation are permitted by Section 6.05. The default is defined by reference to the wrong section.

The proviso allows a cure period "with respect to an Event of Default set forth in clause (vi)," although the provision defines "Master Servicer Events of Termination" and no clause is labelled an Event of Default, and the same sentence both permits ("may") and compels ("shall") the Trustee to terminate. Whether termination is discretionary, and whether the cure right exists, are both open on the words.

This paragraph provides that the Trust Administrator "shall likewise be removed" automatically when a common Master Servicer is terminated, while Section 9.07 provides that in that event "the Depositor shall also remove the Trust Administrator." Automatic removal and removal by act of the Depositor are different mechanisms for the same event.

The successor Trustee's advancing duty is described twice as the "obligation to make Advances pursuant to Section 4.10," but Section 4.10 governs the determination of LIBOR; Advances are required by Section 4.01. The duty the Trustee assumes, and the law-prohibition escape from it, are tied to the wrong section.

This transfer-cost paragraph duplicates the closing paragraphs of Section 3.05 almost word for word, so the same reimbursement right appears in two places. Whether the two are cumulative or a single right is left unresolved.

The prudent-person standard applies only while an Event of Termination is uncured "but only until such time as a successor Master Servicer shall have been appointed," so the heightened duty switches on and off by reference to events the Trustee itself may control. What the Trustee owed at any given moment is a genuine question of construction.

The limitation to "such duties and only such duties as are specifically set forth" is difficult to reconcile with Section 2.06, in which the Trustee agrees to perform its duties "to the best of its ability, to the end that the interests of the Holders ... may be adequately and effectively protected." The instrument states the Trustee's duty in two different ways.

The opening sentence preserves the Trustee's liability for "its own negligent action [and] its own negligent failure to act," but clause (i) then provides that the Trustee "shall not be liable except for the performance of such duties and obligations as are specifically set forth" and that no implied obligations may be read in. The two halves of the same sentence pull against each other.

Clause (iv) conditions any duty to investigate on a written request by Holders "evidencing not less than 25% of the Voting Rights allocated to each Class of Certificates," which read literally requires a 25% holding in every Class rather than 25% overall. The threshold for compelling an investigation is genuinely ambiguous.

The Trust's indemnity is available only where the loss "constitutes an 'unanticipated expense incurred by the REMIC' within the meaning of Treasury Regulations Section 1.860G-1(b)(3)(ii)," a tax concept used here as the boundary of a contractual indemnity. Whether a given litigation expense qualifies is a question the words leave open.

The Trustee must have "a credit rating of at least investment grade" without identifying whose rating, of what obligations, or by which agency, and the closing proviso that the Trustee "cannot be an affiliate of the Master Servicer other than the Trustee in its role as successor to the Master Servicer" does not parse. Eligibility cannot be tested against these words.

The opening words preserve liability for the Trust Administrator's "own negligent action, its own negligent failure to act or its own willful misconduct," while clause (i) says it "shall not be liable except for the performance of such duties and obligations as are specifically set forth" and bars implied obligations. The sentence sets up a standard and then largely withdraws it.

Clause (iv) conditions any duty to investigate on written request by Holders "evidencing not less than 25% of the Voting Rights allocated to each Class of Certificates," which on its face demands a 25% position in every Class rather than 25% in aggregate. The threshold is genuinely ambiguous.

Clause (x) entitles the Trust Administrator to reimbursement of litigation costs "out of the Collection Account," an account the Master Servicer establishes and from which only the Master Servicer may withdraw under Section 3.10(a); the Trust Administrator's withdrawal rights are confined to the Distribution Account by Section 3.10(b). The source of reimbursement is inconsistent with the withdrawal provisions.

The Trust's indemnity reaches only losses that constitute an "unanticipated expense incurred by the REMIC" within the meaning of a Treasury regulation, so a tax concept marks the outer boundary of the Trust Administrator's contractual indemnity. Whether a particular expense falls inside it is left to construction.

This Section requires only "a credit rating of at least investment grade," while Section 9.07 requires the Trust Administrator to be "rated at least 'A/F1' by Fitch ... or the equivalent rating by S&P or Moody's." Two different eligibility standards are set for the same office.

The last sentence terminates the Master Servicer automatically whenever a common Trust Administrator is removed — including removal by 51% of Voting Rights under this Section — although Article VII permits termination of the Master Servicer only on a Master Servicer Event of Termination. The two provisions give inconsistent accounts of when the Master Servicer can be removed.

Clause (iii) requires the Trust Administrator to be rated at least "A/F1" by Fitch or the equivalent by S&P or Moody's, whereas Section 9.06 requires only "a credit rating of at least investment grade." The qualifications for the same office are stated inconsistently in adjoining sections.

Any top-up compensation is the difference from "the current market rate ... as mutually determined by the Trustee and the successor Master Servicer" and "as separately negotiated" between them, so the amount payable depends on a future agreement that the provision does not supply a mechanism to reach. It is an agreement to agree on the Trustee's pay.

In a list of prohibitions each beginning "not," covenant (i) reads "receive any income attributable to any asset which is neither a 'qualified mortgage' nor a 'permitted investment,'" omitting the negative and so appearing to require exactly what the REMIC rules forbid. The missing word reverses the covenant.

Clause (iii) is self-referential: it applies "in all other cases, or in the event that [a party] fails to honor its obligations under the preceding clause (i), (ii) or (iii)," although clause (iii) is the very clause being written. The residual allocation of tax liability cannot be applied as drafted.

The Back-Up Certification is to be given "in the form attached hereto as Exhibit U," but Exhibit U is the Additional Form 10-K Disclosure exhibit, while the Sarbanes-Oxley Certification form is Exhibit N. The certification the parties must deliver is tied to the wrong exhibit.

The Form 15 must be filed "[o]n or prior to January 30 of the first year in which the Trust Administrator is able to do so under applicable law," a condition that identifies neither who decides ability nor by what test. The date of the filing obligation is indeterminate.

Section 1.01 defines the "Optional Termination Date" as the date "specified in Section 10.01(a)," yet this subsection specifies no such date, though the Certificate Margin table steps up by reference to it. The provision that is supposed to supply the date does not.

An Auction Sale may occur only if the price suffices to retire "each class of notes issued pursuant to the Indenture" and amounts owed "to the trustee under the Indenture and the NIMS Insurer," but the Agreement never defines or identifies any Indenture. A condition precedent to the sale of the trust's assets depends on an instrument the contract does not identify.

The conditions turn on notes issued under "the Indenture" and on the NIMS Insurer, neither of which is defined or identified anywhere in the Agreement, while Section 1.03 makes the NIMS Insurer's very existence contingent. The auction machinery cannot be applied without importing an instrument outside the contract.

The Master Servicer's purchase right arises only if "a Majority in Interest of the Class C Certificateholders, as Auction Initiator, has not exercised its rights ... on any Auction Date," a negative condition with no closing date since Auction Dates recur every six months. When the Master Servicer's option becomes exercisable cannot be fixed.

This subsection treats the Auction Initiator as "a Majority in Interest of the Class C Certificateholders," whereas Section 1.01 defines the Auction Initiator as "[t]he Class C Certificateholder," with the Certificate Insurer as fallback. The identity of the party whose inaction triggers the option is stated differently.

Exercise of the Master Servicer's purchase option is conditioned on paying "each class of notes issued pursuant to the Indenture" and amounts owed "to the trustee under the Indenture," but no Indenture is defined or identified in this Agreement. The condition cannot be tested from the instrument itself.

After the notice sequence the Trust Administrator "shall pay to UBS Securities LLC, all such amounts," and "all rights of non-tendering Certificateholders in or to such amounts shall thereupon cease," transferring holders' money to a person who is not a party to the Agreement. Whether that forfeiture operates as written is a question the words invite.

After four specific amendment purposes, clause (v) permits the parties "to modify, alter, amend, add to or rescind any of the terms or provisions contained in this Agreement" without holder consent, a catch-all that swallows the enumerated list subject only to a no-material-adverse-effect opinion that a rating agency letter is deemed to satisfy. The limits on unilateral amendment are exactly what the words leave open.

An unlimited power to "modify, alter, amend, add to or rescind any of the terms" without holder consent is difficult to reconcile with the later paragraph of Section 11.01 requiring the consent of a Majority in Interest of each affected Class, and of each Holder for changes to payment amounts or timing. Read literally the first paragraph makes the consent paragraph unnecessary.

The paragraph permits amendment of Section 9.12 in respect of "the Certification required to be attached [to the Form 10-K] as referenced in Section 9.12(d)," but the Sarbanes-Oxley Certification is required by Section 9.12(b)(iv); Section 9.12(d) deals with late and amended filings. The amendment power points to the wrong subsection.

The opening words require the consent of "the Holders of a Majority in Interest" — 51% — "of each Class of Certificates affected," while clause (ii) requires, for an amendment adversely affecting a Class in any material respect, consent of that Class "evidencing ... Percentage Interests aggregating 66%." Two different consent thresholds are set for what may be the same amendment.

The Opinion of Counsel condition applies to every amendment "other than pursuant to the second preceding paragraph," an antecedent that cannot be identified with confidence given the several amendment paragraphs of Section 11.01. Which amendments escape the condition is unclear.

Recordation is to be directed by "a Majority in Interest of the Certificateholders," but Section 1.01 defines "Majority in Interest" only "[a]s to any Class of Regular Certificates," giving no way to compute a majority across all Certificateholders. The direction mechanism has no defined constituency.

The provision declares the conveyance "an absolute sale" and "not ... a pledge," and then provides that if it is nevertheless held to create a security interest the Agreement "shall be deemed to be a security agreement." Whether the transaction is a sale or a secured loan is a characterisation the provision itself leaves open.

The Section states that "[p]ursuant to Section 6.05, the Master Servicer shall be permitted to pledge its rights as servicer," although Section 6.05 says nothing about pledging, and it conditions any resulting substitution on a successor "meeting the requirements of Sections 6.04 and 7.02," although Section 6.04 governs resignation rather than successor qualifications. The cross-references do not support the rights the sentence purports to confirm.

This Section bars assignment by the Master Servicer "without the prior written consent of the Trustee, the Certificate Insurer and Depositor," while Section 6.05 permits the Master Servicer to "sell, assign or delegate its rights, duties and obligations ... in their entirety" on satisfying rating and net worth conditions and without those consents. The two provisions state different rules for the same act.

The no-action clause bars any suit "upon or under or with respect to this Agreement" unless the Holder has first given notice "of a Master Servicer Event of Termination and of the continuance thereof" and 25% of Voting Rights have demanded action, so on its face a claim having nothing to do with the Master Servicer — such as a repurchase claim against the Transferor — has no available precondition to satisfy. The reach of the bar is precisely what the words leave open.

The bar on holder suits is difficult to square with Section 2.03, which states that cure, repurchase or replacement "shall constitute the sole remedies against the Transferor ... available to Certificateholders," language that assumes holders have remedies to pursue. The two provisions give different accounts of what a Certificateholder may do.

The parties' obligations are to be "supplemented and modified as necessary to be consistent with ... interpretive advice or guidance, convention or consensus among active participants in the asset-backed securities markets, advice of counsel, or otherwise," and performance is owed only "to the extent practicable from a timing and information systems perspective." Neither the content of the duty nor the excuse from it can be determined from the words.

The Certificate Insurer and NIMS Insurer are given the rights of parties "to the same extent as if it were a party hereto," which must be read against Section 1.03, under which the NIMS Insurer has no rights unless it has actually insured notes issued under an Indenture, and against Section 12.07, which terminates the Certificate Insurer's rights. The scope of the third-party rights conferred is qualified elsewhere in ways this Section does not mention.

Giving the Certificate Insurer the right to exercise "all Voting Rights of the Holders of the Insured Certificates" has to be reconciled with the many provisions that measure holder action by percentages of Voting Rights — Sections 7.01, 8.02, 8.07 and 11.08 — and with Section 12.07, which terminates the Insurer's rights. Who may vote the Insured Certificates at a given time is not simply stated.

The preceding paragraph gives the Certificate Insurer the right to exercise all Voting Rights of the Insured Certificates "without any further consent" of the Holders, while this paragraph assumes the Holders still exercise those Voting Rights, subject to the Insurer's prior written consent. The two sentences describe inconsistent allocations of the same votes.

The Policy Payments Account is established for the Holders of Insured Certificates and its funds may not be applied to Trust Fund liabilities, yet the Section 1.01 definition of "Trust Fund" expressly includes the Policy Payments Account "and all amounts deposited therein." The account is inside and outside the Trust Fund at the same time.

The subsection twice measures the withdrawal by "the Insured Amount" due on the Insured Certificates, but "Insured Amount" is not defined in Section 1.01 or anywhere else in the Agreement; the related concept used elsewhere is "Guaranteed Distributions." The amount to be withdrawn rests on an undefined term.

The final sentence turns on reduction of "the Class Certificate Balance of the Insured Certificates," a term the Agreement never defines; Section 1.01 defines "Certificate Principal Balance" and "Class Principal Balance." The measure by which insurer payments are excluded is stated in an undefined term.

The notice duty is triggered by "the occurrence of an Event of Default," but the Agreement defines no Event of Default; Section 7.01 defines only a "Master Servicer Event of Termination" despite its heading. What event starts the Trust Administrator's duty is left to inference.

This subsection defines "Business Day" for Article XII by reference to New York and the Corporate Trust Office cities of the Master Servicer, Trustee or Trust Administrator, while the Section 1.01 definition also captures days on which institutions in Minnesota or Maryland are closed. The same term carries two different meanings in one instrument.

The exclusions refer to "Relief Act Interest Shortfalls," but the Agreement defines only "Relief Act Reduction"; no such shortfall term exists in Section 1.01. What the policy does not cover is expressed in a term the contract does not define.

The Trust Administrator is appointed to administer and make payments under "the Certificate Insurance Policy and the Indemnification Agreement," but no Indemnification Agreement is defined or identified anywhere in this Agreement. The scope of the power of attorney granted rests on an unidentified instrument.

The statement that "[n]either the Certificate Insurance Policy nor the amounts paid on the Certificate Insurance Policy will constitute part of the Trust Fund" contradicts the Section 1.01 definition of Trust Fund, which includes the Policy Payments Account "and all amounts deposited therein." The two provisions cannot both be right about the same funds.

Condition (C) requires repayment of policy draws "plus interest at the Late Payment Rate," but that defined rate is capped by reference to "the Insured Notes" and a maximum "as determined by the Class A Note Insurer," neither of which exists in this Agreement. The date on which the Certificate Insurer's rights cease therefore depends on an amount that cannot be computed.
